Recognize a 600 mL deficit by treating the schedule as 20 hours

question.question: Which description correctly distinguishes PEG from PEJ access?
choices: PEG reaches the stomach; PEJ reaches the jejunum
Both end in the stomach and differ only in insertion technique

teachingReview.heading: Connect the route to its advantages
teachingReview.body: Compared with parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition generally costs less and uses the gastrointestinal tract, helping prevent intestinal atrophy. It also carries lower risks of infection, hyperglycemia, cholelithiasis, and cholestasis. These advantages favor using a usable gut; they do not remove aspiration risk or the need to monitor nutrition and hydration.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: Name where the tube ends
teachingReview.body: A nasogastric tube passes through the nose into the stomach. A gastrostomy reaches the stomach through the skin; PEG denotes a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. A jejunostomy reaches the jejunum, part of the small intestine; PEJ denotes a percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy. Gastric and jejunal access are different destinations, so identify the actual tube tip rather than treating every feeding tube as a nasogastric tube.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: State how a calculated rate is rounded
teachingReview.body: Divide the prescribed daily volume by the actual feeding hours to calculate mL per hour. A hypothetical 1,800 mL target over 22 hours requires 81.818... mL per hour, or 81.8 mL per hour to the nearest tenth. That rounded rate delivers 1,799.6 mL over 22 hours, so it approximates the target rather than equaling it exactly. Use the stated rounding instruction and check the resulting volume; a calculation alone does not establish a safe patient-specific pump setting.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: Read energy from the stated formula label
teachingReview.body: For the nutrition-label calculations used here, carbohydrate and protein provide 4 kcal per gram and fat provides 9 kcal per gram. A hypothetical serving labeled 240 kcal with 16 g protein, 23 g carbohydrate, and 9 g fat supplies 64 kcal from protein, 92 kcal from carbohydrate, and 81 kcal from fat using those factors. Protein contributes 64 divided by the stated 240 kcal times 100, or 26.7% to the nearest tenth. Use the label's declared total when a question asks for the percentage of labeled calories; the simple 4/4/9 sum, 237 kcal in this example, need not exactly match that declared total. Enteral carbohydrate energy must not be confused with the 3.4 kcal per gram used for parenteral dextrose.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: Scale nutrients to the amount actually received
teachingReview.body: Apply the delivered fraction of the labeled serving to its energy and nutrient amounts. If the hypothetical 240 kcal serving above is 240 mL and only 180 mL is delivered, the patient receives 180 divided by 240, or three quarters of a serving: 180 kcal and 12 g protein. Half of the full labeled serving supplies 46 kcal from carbohydrate. Count the amount received after spills or incomplete delivery. These are stated-label exercises; verify the actual product and serving information before calculating a clinical prescription.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: Check liquids as carefully as tablets
teachingReview.body: A liquid oral formulation is not automatically suitable for a feeding tube. Both solid and liquid dosage forms can be incompatible, and drug or nutrient interactions can reduce effect or increase toxicity. Consult the exact product's labeling before choosing a formulation or altering it. Do not add a medication directly to the nutrition formula; an oral route designation alone does not establish tube compatibility.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Complete heading/body individually compared with source. Numeric inputs are hypothetical; numerical outputs independently recalculated. No current branded product composition or patient-specific rate inferred.

teachingReview.heading: Prefer the gut when it is usable
teachingReview.body: Enteral nutrition delivers nutrients through the gastrointestinal tract by mouth or feeding tube. It supports gut structure and function, avoids central venous access, and is generally preferred to parenteral nutrition when digestion and absorption are adequate. It does not replace an oral diet when safe oral intake can meet the patient's needs.
teachingReview.sourceReview: Preference with a usable gut and inadequate safe oral intake; route and gut-integrity benefits agree with book. Aspiration and hydration risks preserved elsewhere.

question.question: A patient receives 60 mL per hour for 24 hours, but the goal is 1,800 mL daily. Which interpretation or management plan is most defensible?
choices: Recognize a 360 mL daily deficit and revise the safe rate or schedule
Recognize a 600 mL deficit by treating the schedule as 20 hours
Recognize a 240 mL deficit by using 65 mL per hour
Conclude that 60 mL per hour for 24 hours already supplies 1,800 mL
question.rationale: The current prescription delivers 60 times 24, or 1,440 mL. Subtract 1,440 mL from the 1,800 mL goal to obtain a 360 mL deficit. Any revised rate or schedule must remain safe for the patient.

question.question: A hypothetical formula label states 240 kcal and 16 g protein per serving. Using 4 kcal per gram of protein, what percentage of the labeled calories comes from protein? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.
question.rationale: Protein supplies 16 times 4, or 64 kcal. Divide 64 by the stated 240 kcal and multiply by 100: 26.666...%, or 26.7%. The denominator is labeled energy, not grams of protein.

question.question: A hypothetical formula serving contains 9 g fat. Using 9 kcal per gram of fat, how much energy comes from fat in that serving?
question.rationale: Multiply 9 g fat by 9 kcal per gram to obtain 81 kcal. The 4 kcal per gram factor applies to protein and enteral carbohydrate; 3.4 kcal per gram is used for parenteral dextrose.

question.question: A hypothetical formula contains 23 g carbohydrate per full serving. If half a serving is delivered, how much carbohydrate energy is received using 4 kcal per gram?
question.rationale: A full serving supplies 23 times 4, or 92 kcal from carbohydrate. Half a serving provides 46 kcal. First identify the nutrient energy, then scale it to the delivered fraction.

question.question: A hypothetical formula label states 240 kcal per 240 mL serving. Of one serving, 60 mL is spilled and the remaining 180 mL is accurately delivered. How much labeled energy is received?
question.rationale: The delivered fraction is 180 divided by 240, or 0.75. Multiply 240 kcal by 0.75 to obtain 180 kcal. The spilled portion is excluded from intake.

question.question: A hypothetical label declares 240 kcal per serving with 16 g protein, 23 g carbohydrate, and 9 g fat. The simple 4/4/9 calculation totals 237 kcal. Which denominator should be used to calculate the percentage of the declared calories supplied by protein?
choices: 237 kcal, replacing the declared total with the calculated sum
48 g, the sum of macronutrient masses
question.rationale: The question asks about declared calories, so use the stated 240 kcal total. Protein energy is 16 times 4, or 64 kcal. Do not silently replace the label denominator because the simple nutrient-factor sum differs.

question.question: A formula runs at 70 mL per hour for 18 hours. What volume is delivered?
question.rationale: Seventy milliliters per hour multiplied by 18 hours equals 1,260 mL.

question.question: A patient receives 1,500 mL of a formula that is 76 percent free water. How much water comes from the formula?
question.rationale: One thousand five hundred milliliters multiplied by 0.76 equals 1,140 mL of free water.

question.question: Which principle most strongly favors enteral over parenteral nutrition?
choices: A usable gastrointestinal tract that cannot be supported adequately by oral intake
A need to bypass all intestinal function
question.rationale: Enteral nutrition is preferred when the gut can safely digest and absorb nutrients but oral intake is inadequate.

It cannot be used with a pump

question.question: Which description correctly distinguishes PEG from PEJ access?
choices: PEG reaches the stomach; PEJ reaches the jejunum
Both end in the stomach and differ only in insertion technique
PEG reaches the jejunum; PEJ reaches the stomach
PEG reaches the stomach; PEJ ends in the duodenum
question.rationale: PEG means percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy and ends in the stomach. PEJ means percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy and ends in the jejunum. Nasogastric access passes through the nose to the stomach.

addedBodies.heading: Connect the route to its advantages
addedBodies.body: Compared with parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition generally costs less and uses the gastrointestinal tract, helping prevent intestinal atrophy. It also carries lower risks of infection, hyperglycemia, cholelithiasis, and cholestasis. These advantages favor using a usable gut; they do not remove aspiration risk or the need to monitor nutrition and hydration.

addedBodies.heading: Name where the tube ends
addedBodies.body: A nasogastric tube passes through the nose into the stomach. A gastrostomy reaches the stomach through the skin; PEG denotes a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. A jejunostomy reaches the jejunum, part of the small intestine; PEJ denotes a percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy. Gastric and jejunal access are different destinations, so identify the actual tube tip rather than treating every feeding tube as a nasogastric tube.

addedBodies.heading: State how a calculated rate is rounded
addedBodies.body: Divide the prescribed daily volume by the actual feeding hours to calculate mL per hour. A hypothetical 1,800 mL target over 22 hours requires 81.818... mL per hour, or 81.8 mL per hour to the nearest tenth. That rounded rate delivers 1,799.6 mL over 22 hours, so it approximates the target rather than equaling it exactly. Use the stated rounding instruction and check the resulting volume; a calculation alone does not establish a safe patient-specific pump setting.

addedBodies.heading: Read energy from the stated formula label
addedBodies.body: For the nutrition-label calculations used here, carbohydrate and protein provide 4 kcal per gram and fat provides 9 kcal per gram. A hypothetical serving labeled 240 kcal with 16 g protein, 23 g carbohydrate, and 9 g fat supplies 64 kcal from protein, 92 kcal from carbohydrate, and 81 kcal from fat using those factors. Protein contributes 64 divided by the stated 240 kcal times 100, or 26.7% to the nearest tenth. Use the label's declared total when a question asks for the percentage of labeled calories; the simple 4/4/9 sum, 237 kcal in this example, need not exactly match that declared total. Enteral carbohydrate energy must not be confused with the 3.4 kcal per gram used for parenteral dextrose.

addedBodies.heading: Scale nutrients to the amount actually received
addedBodies.body: Apply the delivered fraction of the labeled serving to its energy and nutrient amounts. If the hypothetical 240 kcal serving above is 240 mL and only 180 mL is delivered, the patient receives 180 divided by 240, or three quarters of a serving: 180 kcal and 12 g protein. Half of the full labeled serving supplies 46 kcal from carbohydrate. Count the amount received after spills or incomplete delivery. These are stated-label exercises; verify the actual product and serving information before calculating a clinical prescription.

addedBodies.heading: Check liquids as carefully as tablets
addedBodies.body: A liquid oral formulation is not automatically suitable for a feeding tube. Both solid and liquid dosage forms can be incompatible, and drug or nutrient interactions can reduce effect or increase toxicity. Consult the exact product's labeling before choosing a formulation or altering it. Do not add a medication directly to the nutrition formula; an oral route designation alone does not establish tube compatibility.
